result: MS patients showed increased recall error compared to healthy controls across both MGL and sequential paradigms. In the MGL paradigm, SPMS patients had significantly higher recall error than both healthy controls and RRMS patients, while RRMS did not differ from controls. In sequential paradigms (both high and low memory load), both RRMS and SPMS showed significantly higher recall error than controls, with SPMS showing greater impairment than RRMS in the low memory load condition.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted these findings, with one stating the results 'identify a specific decrease in the precision of VWM recall in MS' and another noting 'the strength of evidence for the claims is otherwise convincing.' The overall pattern of increased recall error in MS was not questioned by any reviewer.

result: MS patients demonstrated decreased recall precision compared to healthy controls. In the MGL paradigm, SPMS showed significantly lower precision than both RRMS and controls, while RRMS did not differ from controls. In sequential paradigms, both RRMS and SPMS showed significantly lower precision than controls in both high and low memory load conditions, with SPMS showing greater impairment than RRMS in the low memory load condition.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these precision findings as part of the overall pattern of working memory impairment. One reviewer specifically noted the study 'identify a specific decrease in the precision of VWM recall in MS,' directly supporting these claims. No concerns were raised about the precision measurements.

result: Computational modeling using von Mises distribution showed that the circular standard deviation of recall error was significantly higher in MS patients compared to controls in both high and low memory load conditions. Both RRMS and SPMS showed increased von Mises SD compared to controls, with SPMS showing greater impairment than RRMS in the low memory load condition.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the computational modeling approach and results without raising concerns. One reviewer specifically praised 'the application of more precise psychophysiological methods' and noted the use of 'mixture modelling to disentangle different contributions to overall performance,' indicating acceptance of these modeling results.

result: Computational modeling identified that imprecision in decoding information and swap error (mistakenly reporting features of other presented items) were responsible for WM dysfunction in MS. Target response proportion was lower and swap error was higher in MS patients compared to controls in the high memory load condition.
evaluation: While reviewers accepted the overall findings, one reviewer explicitly noted 'the possibility that visual and/or motor impairments contribute to performance decrements on the memory task cannot be ruled out,' raising uncertainty about whether the observed swap errors and imprecision definitively reflect WM dysfunction versus other confounding factors.

result: Uniform response proportion (random responses) was higher in MS patients compared to controls in the high memory load condition, with both RRMS and SPMS showing increased uniform responses compared to healthy controls.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about the uniform response findings. These results were part of the accepted mixture modeling approach that one reviewer praised for its ability to 'disentangle different contributions to overall performance.'

result: ROC analysis showed that sequential paradigms were better at distinguishing healthy controls from RRMS (79-86% accuracy), while the MGL paradigm was more accurate in discriminating MS subtypes (SPMS from RRMS, 84.7% accuracy). The MGL paradigm showed poor ability to distinguish healthy controls from RRMS (64.1%).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these discriminative findings without raising concerns. The overall assessment that 'the strength of evidence for the claims is otherwise convincing' and that the paper 'provides valuable information' supports acceptance of these ROC analysis results showing differential diagnostic utility of the paradigms.

result: The authors interpret their findings as indicating hippocampal disruption in SPMS patients and suggest that spatial WM assessment could be a specific marker for WM system disorganization in SPMS. They also propose that parietal regions and globus pallidus could be candidate regions responsible for observed impairments in conjunctive processing.
evaluation: These are speculative interpretations based on inference from the data and cited literature. While reviewers did not explicitly challenge these interpretations, one reviewer noted 'the possibility that visual and/or motor impairments contribute to performance decrements' cannot be ruled out, suggesting caution about neuroanatomical interpretations. These claims go beyond what the behavioral data alone can support.

result: Background claims about MS, working memory, continuous reproduction paradigms, and previous findings in other neurological disorders, all supported by citations to existing literature.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these background claims, which are standard knowledge supported by appropriate citations. One reviewer noted the study 'represents an advance beyond prior work in this area,' implicitly accepting the characterization of previous research.

result: Methodological details including participant numbers, recruitment procedures, diagnostic criteria, exclusion criteria, cognitive assessment tools, and ethical approvals.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged 'some weaknesses with the way the clinical groups were matched, but those limitations are acknowledged,' indicating they accepted the methodological details while noting limitations. The overall assessment that evidence is 'convincing' suggests acceptance of the basic methodological framework.
